title: The power of persuasion
goals: Connect ideas precisely using discourse markers: nevertheless, on the contrary, by the same token, albeit, hence.
Distinguish nuances between markers that seem equivalent (on the contrary vs. on the other hand, albeit vs. although).
Condense and formalise information through nominalisation, using the correct prepositions.
Choose the appropriate register (formal, semi-formal, informal) according to the reader and the purpose.
Talk about media and advertising: bias, spin, clickbait, credibility, fact-checking.
Analyse arguments and write a well-structured persuasive text.

learn.title: Discourse markers: contrast, concession, addition and consequence
learn.html:
At C1 level, but, and and so are no longer enough. An advanced text relies on markers that signal how each idea relates to the previous one, and that choose the exact nuance: contradicting is not the same as qualifying, and adding an argument is not the same as reinforcing it with the same logic.

FunctionMarkersNuance and use
Contrasthowever, nevertheless, nonetheless, even so, that saidThey introduce a fact that clashes with what came before but does not cancel it. Nevertheless / nonetheless are more formal; that said and even so sound more natural in speech.
Contraston the other hand / in contrast / whereas / whileThey compare two viewpoints or two realities. Whereas and while join two clauses into a single sentence.
Rejectionon the contraryIt is NOT the same as "on the other hand". It denies what has just been said (or assumed) and affirms the opposite: It isn't a failure. On the contrary, it's a success.
Concessionadmittedly, granted, albeit, notwithstandingAdmittedly / granted acknowledge a point from the other side before counterarguing. Albeit (= "although") is followed by an adjective or a short phrase, not a full clause: a good, albeit expensive, solution. Notwithstanding works as a preposition ("despite").
Additionmoreover, furthermore, what is more, besides, by the same tokenMoreover / furthermore add a stronger argument. By the same token adds something that follows from the same logic ("for the same reason, in the same way").
Consequenceconsequently, as a result, hence, thus, therebyHence is very formal and is followed by a noun or a short phrase. Thereby + -ing expresses the result of an action: …cutting costs, thereby raising profits.
Clarification / examplein other words, namely, for instance, a case in pointNamely specifies (it identifies exact elements); in other words reformulates.

Punctuation. Adverbial markers usually go at the start and are followed by a comma, or come after a semicolon: The ad was effective; nevertheless, it was withdrawn. They can also go in the middle of the sentence, between commas: The ad, however, was withdrawn. Avoid using two markers at once for the same relationship (Although… however).

Register. Furthermore, nonetheless, hence are typical of formal written texts; in a conversation or an informal email they sound stilted. There, besides, still, even so, that said, so work better.

watch.wrong: The plan is cheap. On the contrary, it has serious flaws.
watch.right: The plan is cheap. On the other hand, it has serious flaws.
watch.why: On the contrary negates the previous statement; here only a contrast is being added, so on the other hand is the right choice.

watch.wrong: Although he was tired, however he kept working.
watch.right: Although he was tired, he kept working. / He was tired; however, he kept working.
watch.why: A conjunction and a connector should not be combined to express the same idea of contrast.

watch.wrong: Albeit he was exhausted, he finished the talk.
watch.right: Albeit exhausted, he finished the talk.
watch.why: Albeit does not introduce a clause with a subject and a verb; it goes with an adjective, a participle or a short phrase.

watch.wrong: In the other hand, the results are encouraging.
watch.right: On the other hand, the results are encouraging.
watch.why: The fixed expression is on the other hand (with on, not in).

learn.title: Nominalisation: turning actions and qualities into nouns
learn.html:
Nominalisation means expressing with a noun what we would normally say with a verb or an adjective: People distrust the media → There is widespread distrust of the media. It is one of the most recognisable features of formal and academic written English, and it is essential in TOEFL-style essays.

Clause (more spoken)Nominalisation (more formal)
Prices rose sharply, which worried consumers.The sharp rise in prices worried consumers.
Governments decided to regulate platforms.The decision to regulate platforms was controversial.
Readers are aware that headlines can mislead.Awareness that headlines can mislead is growing.
It is important to verify sources.The importance of verifying sources cannot be overstated.

Common endings: -tion/-sion (decision, persuasion), -ment (manipulation, endorsement), -ence/-ance (reliance, influence), -ity/-ness (credibility, awareness), -al (refusal, approval), -ure (failure, exposure). Some nouns are identical to the verb (a rise, a cut, an increase) and others change completely (fail → failure, believe → belief).

What it is for: it condenses information (a noun can sum up an entire clause), gives an impersonal, objective tone and allows long, complex subjects. The price is density: too many nominalisations in a row make a text heavy. Balance them with action verbs: lead to, give rise to, account for, contribute to (The spread of misinformation has given rise to a crisis of trust).

Prepositions that go with the noun (different from those of the original verb, and sometimes different from Spanish): an increase/rise/decline in, demand for, reliance on, impact/influence on, solution to, attitude to/towards, a lack of, a tendency to, the failure to + verb.

watch.wrong: There was a sharp increase of prices.
watch.right: There was a sharp increase in prices.
watch.why: An increase "in" something: increase/rise/fall in. Of is used for quantities: an increase of 5%.

watch.wrong: The importance of to be informed is clear.
watch.right: The importance of being informed is clear.
watch.why: After a preposition the verb takes -ing, not the infinitive.

watch.wrong: The influence of social media in voters is huge.
watch.right: The influence of social media on voters is huge.
watch.why: The preposition used with influence/impact/effect is on.

watch.wrong: Their refusal of cooperate surprised us.
watch.right: Their refusal to cooperate surprised us.
watch.why: Refusal, decision, failure and attempt take to + verb, just like the verbs they come from.

learn.title: Formal vs. informal register
learn.html:
Mastering English at C1 means knowing when to say something, not just how. Register depends on three things: your relationship with the listener or reader, the medium (spoken or written) and the purpose. An email to a friend, a letter of complaint and an academic essay each call for a different kind of English.

FeatureInformal / neutralFormal
Verbslook into, put up with, go up, find out, turn downinvestigate, tolerate, rise, ascertain, reject
Quantifiersa lot of, loads of, kidsa considerable number of, numerous, children
Connectorsbut, so, plus, anywayhowever, therefore, moreover, nevertheless
Structurecontractions, active voice, I thinkno contractions, passive and impersonal constructions (It is widely believed that…), abstract nouns
PolitenessCan you send me…? / Sorry about that.I would be grateful if you could…; We apologise for any inconvenience.

Watch the extremes. More formal does not mean better. An overly elaborate register (I would be most grateful were you to forward the aforementioned document to a colleague) sounds pompous, even ironic. And in a persuasive text the register is usually semi-formal: precise vocabulary, but with devices that connect with the reader, such as the rhetorical question, the triad of ideas (faster, cheaper, fairer) or the short contrast.

Coherence. The real problem is not being formal or informal, but mixing registers without intent: Dear Sir, I wanna complain about your totally awesome mistake is incoherent. In a TOEFL essay, avoid contractions, colloquial expressions and the generic you; but do not pile up nominalisations until nobody can read the text.

watch.wrong: Dear Sir, I wanna complain because your ad is kinda misleading.
watch.right: Dear Sir, I am writing to complain that your advertisement is misleading.
watch.why: A formal letter does not use wanna, kinda or other colloquial contractions.

watch.wrong: Loads of people think that kids are easily persuaded.
watch.right: Many people believe that children are easily persuaded.
watch.why: An academic text prefers many / numerous and children.

watch.wrong: You can see that advertising has a big effect on people.
watch.right: It can be argued that advertising has a considerable effect on people.
watch.why: The generic you is avoided; the impersonal construction gives objectivity.

watch.wrong: I would be most grateful if you could pass me the salt, my dear friend.
watch.right: Could you pass me the salt, please?
watch.why: A register that is too formal for the situation sounds artificial or sarcastic.

learn.title: Analysing and presenting arguments
learn.html:
• The author's central claim is that… — identifying the thesis of a text.
  • This argument rests on the assumption that… — pointing out the implicit assumption.
  • A case in point is… — introducing a representative example.
  • Admittedly, … ; that said, … — conceding a point and counterarguing.
  • That is not to say that… — avoiding an exaggerated interpretation: That is not to say that all ads are dishonest.
  • It would be naive to suppose that… — rejecting an idea politely.
  • I would argue that… / It could be argued that… — presenting your opinion with some distance.
  • Taken at face value, … ; however, a closer look reveals… — separating appearance from analysis.
  • By the same token, … / Equally, … — applying the same reasoning to another case.
  • To put it another way, … / In other words, … — reformulating.

write.prompt: Write a persuasive text of 250 to 350 words for a university magazine, titled 'Should we trust what we read online?'. Present your position, develop at least two arguments with examples, acknowledge and refute an objection, and close with a call to action. Use a semi-formal register.
checklist: Clear thesis in the introduction
At least 5 different markers (nevertheless, on the contrary, by the same token, admittedly, hence…)
Correct use of on the contrary vs. on the other hand
At least 4 nominalisations with the correct preposition (increase in, reliance on, influence on…)
A rhetorical question or a triad to persuade
Concession and refutation of an objection
Consistent register, with no colloquialisms or mixed styles
Between 250 and 350 words
write.model:
Should we trust what we read online?

Every day, most of us read dozens of articles, posts and headlines, and we trust many of them without a second thought. My position is simple: we should read online content with curiosity, but not with blind faith.

The first reason is the sheer scale of misinformation. There has been a dramatic increase in the volume of false stories circulating on social media, and the speed at which they spread far exceeds that of any correction. Our reliance on a handful of platforms, whose algorithms reward outrage rather than accuracy, only makes matters worse. Hence the real danger is not that we are lied to, but that we are rarely invited to doubt.

Secondly, the influence of repetition on our beliefs is well documented. A claim that we see ten times begins to feel familiar, and familiarity is easily mistaken for truth. By the same token, a decline in trust in traditional institutions has left many readers looking for comfort in sources that merely confirm what they already think.

Admittedly, it could be objected that the internet has also democratised knowledge. Anyone can now read a scientific paper, watch a lecture from a leading university or hear voices that were once excluded from the media. That is true, but it does not follow that every source is equally reliable. On the contrary, the abundance of information makes judgement more important, not less. Freedom to publish is valuable; on the other hand, it places a heavier burden on the reader.

So what should we do? Check the source, compare the evidence and pause before sharing. Be sceptical, be fair and be patient. Nevertheless, scepticism is not cynicism: if each of us took thirty seconds to verify a story before sharing it, the effect on public debate would be enormous. Let us start today.

write.prompt: In writing (250 to 300 words), analyse an advert, a headline or a real speech that you know: identify the central claim, the persuasive devices (emotive language, bandwagon, cherry-picking…) and assess whether the argument is credible. End with your personal evaluation.
checklist: Summary of the central claim (The central claim is…)
At least two persuasive devices named and explained
An analytical expression (rests on the assumption that, taken at face value…)
Concession with admittedly / granted and contrast with that said / however
Justified final evaluation
Formal-neutral register, no contractions
Between 250 and 300 words
write.model:
The advert I have chosen is a familiar one for a breakfast cereal, which claims that "nine out of ten families who tried it now choose it every morning". The central claim is that this cereal is the preferred choice of the great majority of families and, by implication, that it is therefore a healthy and sensible product.

The advert relies on several persuasive devices. The first is the bandwagon appeal: the phrase "nine out of ten families" invites viewers to join a crowd and suggests that not buying the product would make them an exception. The second is cherry-picking. The statistic refers only to families who tried it, so those who disliked it and never bought it again are quietly excluded, and no information is given about the size or selection of the sample. Emotive language reinforces the effect, since images of laughing children and sunlit kitchens associate the cereal with happiness rather than with nutrition.

Taken at face value, the claim sounds impressive. However, it rests on the assumption that popularity is evidence of quality, which is clearly questionable. Moreover, the advert never mentions the sugar content, which is the very information a health-conscious parent would need.

Admittedly, the advert is skilfully made, and it is not entirely dishonest: it may well be true that many families enjoy the product. Granted, enjoyment is a legitimate reason to buy a cereal. That said, the argument does not establish what it implies, namely that the product is good for children.

In my evaluation, the advert is persuasive but not credible. It succeeds in appealing to emotion, yet it fails as an argument, and a careful consumer should treat it with caution.

reading.title: Who is really persuading whom?
reading.intro: Read the essay and answer the questions.
paragraphs: Every morning, before most of us have finished our first coffee, we have already been persuaded of something. A headline nudged us to feel outraged; a sponsored post suggested a product we had not known we needed; a friend's shared video convinced us, for a few seconds at least, that the world was either on fire or magnificently fine. Persuasion is not an occasional event in modern life but its constant background noise, and the sophisticated consumer of media is not the person who resists it entirely, which is impossible, but the one who notices it.

Consider the humble headline. Editors have always known that a title is an advertisement for the story beneath it, yet the economics of online publishing have pushed the practice to extremes. Revenue depends on clicks, and clicks depend on curiosity, anger or fear. Hence the proliferation of headlines that promise revelations they never deliver. Defenders of the practice argue that readers are not fools and that a catchy title is harmless provided the article is accurate. Admittedly, there is something in this. However, research on reading habits suggests that a large share of people never get past the headline at all, and for them the headline is the story. If it distorts, the distortion is the only version of events they receive.

Bias is a subtler matter, because it rarely takes the form of outright falsehood. More often it operates through selection and framing: which facts are included, which are buried in the twelfth paragraph, which adjectives accompany which names. Compare 'protesters clashed with police' and 'police cracked down on protesters'. Both may be literally true; neither is neutral. Politicians, of course, have turned such choices into a profession. Spin doctors do not lie so much as arrange the truth into a flattering shape, describing a cut as a 'savings opportunity' and a failure as a 'valuable lesson'. The reader who spots the framing is already half protected.

It would be comforting to believe that the remedy is simply more information, but the evidence is discouraging. People tend to seek out sources that confirm what they already think, and algorithms, designed to keep us engaged, oblige them. The result is the so-called echo chamber, in which one's views come back amplified and unchallenged. Fact-checking organisations do valuable work, yet corrections rarely travel as far or as fast as the original claim, and a retraction published on page nine does little to undo a headline seen by millions. Nor is scepticism a cure-all: when everything is suspect, nothing is credible, and a cynical shrug can be exactly what a manipulator hopes for.

What, then, can be done? The most promising answer is neither censorship nor naive trust but habit. Ask who is speaking and what they stand to gain. Look for the evidence behind a claim rather than the confidence with which it is delivered. Notice emotive language, and ask what it is doing in place of an argument. And, by the same token, apply the same scrutiny to the messages we agree with, since those are the ones we are least inclined to question. None of this makes persuasion go away, nor should it; a good argument deserves to persuade. The aim is not to become immune but to become a harder audience: one that can be convinced by reasons, and is rather less easily moved by tricks.

a rapid increase in number or amount
a cure-all; a solution supposed to fix every problem
protected from something; not affected by it

listening.title: Why do we fall for clickbait?
listening.intro: Listen to the radio programme with a guest and a listener. You can repeat it.

lines.text: Welcome back to The Daily Lens. Today we're asking a simple question: why do we keep falling for clickbait? With me is media-literacy teacher Dr Elena Reyes. Elena, welcome.
Thanks for having me. Though I'd say 'falling for' is a bit harsh. These headlines are engineered by people who study our psychology for a living.
Fair enough. But surely we're not that gullible?
Gullible, no. Busy, yes. We read the headline, glance at the picture, and move on. That's precisely what the industry counts on.
We have a caller on the line. Marcos, you're on air.
Hi there. I work in digital marketing, and I have to say, clickbait gets a bad press. If the article delivers, what's the harm?
Fair point, Marcos, and I'd concede that some curiosity-driven headlines are harmless. That said, the problem arises when the headline promises far more than the story contains.
Sure, but it's up to readers to think critically, isn't it? I mean, nobody forces them to click.

On the contrary, the whole design is meant to make clicking feel automatic. By the same token, you wouldn't blame shoppers for impulse buys at the checkout, would you? The shelf is arranged to tempt them.
That's a good analogy. So what should listeners actually do?

Three quick habits. First, check who published it and whether you've heard of them. Second, look for a named source rather than 'experts say'. Third, pause before sharing, because outrage travels faster than accuracy.
I'll admit that last one hits home. I shared something last week that turned out to be a hoax.
You're in good company, Marcos. Elena, thank you, and Marcos, thanks for being honest about it.
Anytime. And remember, a retraction never gets as many views as the original mistake.

tasks.prompt: Analyse an advert or a headline you have seen: what persuasion technique does it use, and does it work on you?
questions: Can you describe an advert or headline that caught your attention recently?
What persuasion technique does it use?
Does it work on you? Why, or why not?
Is it ethical, in your view?
tasks.model: A headline I saw last week said 'Doctors hate this simple trick'. It's classic clickbait: it promises a secret and plays on curiosity. Admittedly, it worked on me for about ten seconds, since I clicked. Nevertheless, the article contained nothing new, so I felt manipulated. In my view it's borderline unethical, because it deliberately exploits our curiosity without delivering anything of value.
checklist: Name the technique (clickbait, bandwagon, emotive language…)
At least two markers (admittedly, nevertheless, however…)
Justified opinion with because / since
Media vocabulary from the block

tasks.prompt: Argue for or against: 'Advertising does more harm than good.' Present an argument, concede a point and counterargue.
questions: Do you agree that advertising does more harm than good?
What is the strongest argument on the other side?
Is there a type of advertising you think is acceptable?
Who should be responsible for regulating it?
tasks.model: I'd argue that advertising does more harm than good, at least in its current form. It encourages consumption we don't need and targets vulnerable groups such as children. That said, I'd concede that it funds a great deal of free content and helps small businesses reach customers. By the same token, however, we should ask who benefits most: usually large corporations. On balance, I think stricter regulation is the answer, rather than a ban.
checklist: Clear thesis (I'd argue that…)
Concession + counterargument (admittedly / that said)
By the same token, or another addition connector
Conclusion with On balance / Overall

tasks.prompt: Register role-play: first, persuade a friend to use their phone less (informal); then ask your boss to reschedule a meeting (formal).
questions: Friend: Why are you telling me to put my phone down?
Friend: But I'm only checking the news!
Manager: You wanted to see me about something?
Manager: Why can't the meeting stay at ten?
tasks.model: Friend version: Look, I'm not saying you're addicted, but you've checked it five times since we sat down. Give it a rest, will you? Manager version: Thank you for seeing me. I was wondering whether it would be possible to move tomorrow's meeting to eleven, as I have a prior commitment. I apologise for any inconvenience this may cause, and I would be happy to adjust my schedule in return.
checklist: Informal register: contractions, colloquial expressions
Formal register: I was wondering whether…, I would be happy to…
Appropriate politeness in the request
Clear shift between the two registers
